extracted.intended_audience: Variety/entertainment readers; late-night TV viewers and followers of political comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and examples for producing/evaluating late-night monologue political comedy as illustrated by Stephen Colbert's monologue responding to Trump and his show's cancellation. Focuses on comedic devices, topicality, audience engagement, and industry-aware framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mock outrage as setup
rubrics_metrics.description: With mock outrage, Colbert said, 'How dare you, sir? Would an untalented man be able to compose the following satirical witticism?'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use feigned indignation to frame a joke and set up a punchline; the article presents 'mock outrage' as an opening rhetorical move that primes the audience for satire and contrast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing device / 'Eloquence Cam' and affected accent
rubrics_metrics.description: Colbert appeared in an on-screen frame that said 'Eloquence Cam' and, staring directly into the camera, affected a clipped New York accent: 'Go fuck yourself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employing a named on-screen gimmick and a deliberately affected voice can heighten the comedic payoff — the piece highlights the 'Eloquence Cam' bit as an explicit device to land the line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bleeped profanity as comic emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: The f-bomb was bleeped out, and the line drew a massive roar of approval from the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Censoring profanity (bleeps) can serve as an audible punchline and rally the audience; the article uses the bleep to underline the shock/value while keeping broadcast standards in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-martyrdom / grand metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: Colbert quipped, 'Kimmel, I am the martyr. There’s only room for one on this cross. And the view is fantastic from up here.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopting an exaggerated 'martyr' persona and extended metaphor (cross/martyrdom) can be used to comically position the host in relation to peers and opponents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understated ('milquetoast') critique as inversion
rubrics_metrics.description: He offered this comically milquetoast critique of Trump: 'I don’t care for him. Doesn’t have the skillset to be president. Not a good fit, that’s all.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delivering an intentionally tame or mild critique — especially after heated buildup — can produce irony and laughs by subverting expectations of escalation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing gratitude/praise with satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Colbert reiterated his praise for CBS, saying they have 'always been great partners,' even while criticizing the cancellation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixing genuine gratitude for institutions/partners with satirical commentary lets the comedian critique while maintaining professional decorum and audience sympathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topical/current-events tying for punchlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Colbert referenced the Paramount-Trump settlement, the timing of the cancellation, and reports about program losses to contextualize jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground jokes in current news (settlements, industry events) to make satire timely and consequential; the article shows linking jokes to recent developments heightens perceived relevance and sting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using audience reaction and crowd energy
rubrics_metrics.description: The bleeped line 'drew a massive roar of approval from the audience' and guests/attendees chanted/cheered during taping; protesters gathered outside shouting support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on live audience responses (cheers, chants, boos) to build momentum and signal punchline success; visible crowd energy amplifies broadcast impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cameos and spoof videos to amplify message
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Late Show' features cameos by Jimmy Fallon, Jon Stewart, John Oliver, Seth Meyers, Adam Sandler and more in spoofs (e.g., Coldplay Kiss-Cam video).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use celebrity cameos and pre-taped spoofs to broaden reach, create viral moments, and generate solidarity among peers — the article points to cameo-filled spoofs as part of the show's response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta/industry-aware jokes (contracts & timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Variety explains networks announce cancellations when they do because late-night writers/producers sign one-year deals; Colbert noted he found out the night before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate industry realities (contract cycles, corporate timing) into jokes to add insider texture and justify timing or tone of the material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guest voices as vehicles for collective sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: When Sandra Oh came on stage she said: 'I’m so sorry, and saddened, and properly outraged for the cancellation of late night here.' She added: 'To CBS and Paramount: a plague on both of your houses.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use guest remarks to articulate audience/industry feelings, amplifying outrage or sympathy and lending additional authority/emotion to the host's position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social media previews/captions to frame comedic tone
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Late Show' posted a preview on Instagram with the caption: 'Sticks and stones may break our bones but presidential turds can never hurt us.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage social platforms and provocative captions to set audience expectations and extend the joke beyond broadcast; teasers can frame how viewers interpret the show’s stance.
